paragraphs.source_en: Whether it was selective hunting, pre-domestication or another reason for the predominance of mouflon remains in the North African and Central Saharan sites, it certainly testifies to the importance of this animal. The Iberomaurusian site of Taforalt may indicate that this importance was not purely a practical one but that a deeper meaning lies behind the presence of mouflon remains. At Taforalt an Epipalaeolithic burial was marked by mouflon horns which indicates the connection of this animal to the dead person or perhaps to death in general. Another Iberomaurusian site, Tamar Hat, revealed one of the oldest datable art objects found in the Sahara dated to the 20th millennium BP (Aumassip 1986).

paragraphs.source_en: It is an engraved stone in the form of mouflon horns and it confirms that not only did the mouflon and its horns occupy an important place in the ideology but also that this ideology has very ancient roots stretching back to at least the 20th millennium BP. The Iberomaurusian burial and art do not seem to be directly related to the rock art in the Central Sahara, however, the importance mouflon has in the art and ideology suggests a similar cultural development throughout the Early Holocene hunter-gatherers in different regions of the Sahara.

paragraphs.source_en: Parietal rock art is unknown in the Iberomaurusian culture perhaps because it lacks suitable rocks (Aumassip 1986); the art is nevertheless perceptible in portable objects. In the Central Saharan mountains no pre-Pastoral portable art was found but it is possible that with such a large number of suitable walls the prehistoric hunters focused on parietal art. More than one hundred paintings of mouflon, often of large dimensions, with elaborated horns and sometimes decorated in the same way as the anthropomorphic figures, indicates the symbolical, rather than practical significance of this animal.

paragraphs.source_en: Further evidence of the importance of mouflon is provided by the Uan Afuda shelter in the Acacus, which is decorated with the Round Head anthropomorphic figures in association with mouflon. A group of antelope and mouflon are aligned in the same direction towards the East. The human figures are mixed with the animals, however, it is not a hunting scene and it does not seem to be a ritual scene either, rather the animals and humans appear to be shown in an attitude of a harmonious interaction, even though different periods of painting cannot be excluded (Di Lernia 1999).
